passage:
At two, Payal held out her wooden giraffe to her uncle after he handed her a picture book, then hugged his knee. Her mother whispered, "Say thank you," and Payal chirped it back, beaming at the book more than at the words.

At fifteen, she sent hearts and a row of clapping emojis under her friend Sangeeta's post about the school play, and then paused. It felt a bit easy. She typed a separate message: "The way you held the last note when your voice shook made me cry. You did that so well." Sangeeta replied in seconds: "You have no idea how much I needed that. 🙂"

At twenty-five, in a team meeting, Payal said, "Before I present the numbers, Binita found the error in our first draft last Thursday and rebuilt the whole sheet over the weekend. Without her, this would have been wrong." Binita looked up, surprised, and smiled.

qa.q: What did Payal hand over to her uncle at two?
qa.a: Payal handed her uncle her wooden giraffe.

qa.q: How does Payal's way of showing appreciation develop from two to fifteen to twenty-five?
qa.a: At two she gives a toy and a hug and repeats a prompted thank you, at fifteen she moves from quick hearts to a specific personal message, and at twenty-five she gives specific, public credit for Binita's real work in a meeting.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she replied that Payal had no idea how much she needed the message?
qa.a: Sangeeta was moved and grateful, feeling that the specific message meant more than a row of reactions.

qa.q: Why did Payal's credit for Binita work well?
qa.a: It was specific, timely and public, naming what Binita did and when, so Binita felt recognised and the team saw the real contribution.

grounding: Appreciation and recognition at three ages: a toddler's thank-you gestures, a teenager's shift from reactions to a specific message, and a young professional crediting a teammate in public.
